source_refs.note: Chapter 12 exercise (PDF 276-279, printed 273-276): MCQs keyed from the chapter (the book prints no key), model answers to the written questions, numericals worked step by step and checked against the printed answers; corrections in the lesson.

blocks.prompt: 12.1 Which one of the following is the fundamental particle:
blocks.explanation: A fundamental particle has no internal structure. The electron is a lepton, which is fundamental; protons and neutrons are made of three quarks and mesons of a quark and an antiquark (Section 12.5).

blocks.prompt: 12.2 The first discovered anti-particle is:
blocks.explanation: The antielectron (positron) was the first anti-particle discovered, by Anderson in 1932 in a cloud chamber; the anti-proton came in 1955 (Section 12.3).

blocks.prompt: 12.3 Which one of the following pair of particles creates annihilation:
blocks.explanation: Annihilation happens when a particle meets its own anti-particle: e⁻ + e⁺ → γ + γ.

blocks.prompt: 12.4 The strong nuclear force between the two particles is mediated by:
blocks.explanation: In the chapter (12.7, 12.11) the strong nuclear force is mediated by field particles called gluons; photons carry the electromagnetic force and gravitons gravity. (In the older Yukawa picture the force between two nucleons was described by exchange of mesons (pions); this is beyond the chapter.)

blocks.prompt: 12.5 Which one of the following forces interacts between two particles through photons:
blocks.explanation: Photons are the quanta of the electromagnetic field; charged particles exchange photons (Section 12.11).

blocks.prompt: 12.6 When a neutron changes into a proton then we will observe:
blocks.explanation: In β⁻-decay a neutron changes into a proton: ¹₀n → ¹₁p + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄.

blocks.prompt: 12.7 Baryon is formed by combination of:
blocks.explanation: Baryons (e.g. proton uud, neutron udd) are made of three quarks; a quark-antiquark pair makes a meson.

blocks.prompt: 12.8 Which one of the following forces has negligible effect between the elementary particles:
blocks.explanation: Gravity is the weakest force (about 10⁻³⁸ of the strong force); at the subatomic level its effect is negligible.

blocks.prompt: 12.9 Which particles are produced by strong interaction:
blocks.explanation: Particles that take part in the strong interaction are hadrons (baryons and mesons). Mesons are only one kind of hadron, so (c) is the complete answer; leptons do not feel the strong force.

blocks.prompt: 12.10 A strong nuclear force exists between the nucleons of:
blocks.explanation: The strong nuclear force attracts all nucleons alike: proton-proton, neutron-neutron and proton-neutron.

blocks.prompt: 12.11 Which one of the following radiation/particles has the highest ionization power:
blocks.explanation: α-particles ionize most: about 10⁴ ion pairs per mm in air, against about 10² for β and about 1 for γ (Table 12.2).

blocks.prompt: 12.12 Which one of the following radiation/particles has the highest penetrating power
blocks.explanation: γ-rays have the highest penetrating power: they need 1-10 cm of lead to be absorbed, while α is stopped by paper and β by a few mm of aluminium.

blocks.prompt: 12.13 A change occurs in atomic member of a nucleus but its mass number remains the same by decay of
blocks.explanation: ('atomic member' means atomic number.) In β-decay a neutron changes into a proton (or a proton into a neutron), so Z changes by one while A stays the same. α-decay changes both, γ-decay changes neither.

blocks.prompt: 12.14 In a nucleus, a neutron changes into a proton the atomic number changes by one, the mass number will be
blocks.explanation: No nucleon is lost in β-decay; one nucleon only changes its type, so the mass number A remains the same.

blocks.prompt: 12.15 The electroweak theory was introduced by:
blocks.explanation: Dr. Abdus Salam (with Weinberg and Glashow) unified the electromagnetic and weak forces into the electroweak theory and shared the 1979 Nobel Prize (beyond the chapter: the chapter names the electroweak carriers W⁺, W⁻ and Z but not the theory's authors). Dirac predicted anti-particles; Anderson discovered the positron.

blocks.prompt: 12.16 The asymmetry of matter and antimatter is due to imbalance number of:
blocks.explanation: Section 12.9: the matter-antimatter asymmetry is due to the violation of conservation of baryon number, i.e. an imbalance in the number of baryons and anti-baryons.

blocks.prompt: 12.17 Which one of the following particle is responsible for the mass of the fundamental particle:
blocks.explanation: Particles get mass by interacting with the Higgs field; its particle, the Higgs boson, was discovered in 2012 at CERN (Section 12.7).

blocks.prompt: 12.18 A proton is composed of up and down quarks, the order of quarks is:
blocks.explanation: A proton is uud (two up and one down quark): q = 2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3 = +1. udd is the neutron (q = 0). (udu has the same quarks, but the standard way of writing the proton is uud.)

blocks.prompt: 12.19 The number of quarks that composed of a neutron is:
blocks.explanation: A neutron is a baryon made of three quarks, udd: q = 2/3 − 1/3 − 1/3 = 0.

blocks.prompt: 12.1 What do different isotopes of a given element have in common? How are they different?
blocks.explanation:
Common: the same number of protons (same atomic number Z), so they are the same element with the same chemical symbol.
Different: the number of neutrons, so their mass number A and mass differ; some are stable and some unstable. E.g. ¹²₆C, ¹³₆C (stable) and ¹⁴₆C (radioactive).

blocks.prompt: 12.2 Identify the element that has 87 nucleons and 50 neutrons.
blocks.explanation:
A = 87, N = 50
Z = A − N = 87 − 50 = 37
The element with Z = 37 is rubidium: ⁸⁷₃₇Rb (identifying the element from Z uses the periodic table; beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: 12.3 What are the similarities and differences between the strong nuclear force and the electric force?
blocks.explanation: Similarities: both are fundamental forces, both act between protons, and both are carried by exchange particles (gluons and photons). The differences are in the table.

rows: Very short range (< 10⁻¹⁵ m), only inside the nucleus
Acts on all nucleons, charged or not (p-p, n-n, p-n)

blocks.prompt:
12.4 Fill in the missing particle or nucleus:
a. ⁴⁵₂₀Ca → ? + e⁻ + ν̄
b. ⁵⁸₂₉Cu* → ? + γ
blocks.explanation:
a. β⁻-decay: A stays 45 and Z rises by one to 21 (scandium):
⁴⁵₂₀Ca → ⁴⁵₂₁Sc + e⁻ + ν̄
b. γ-decay: the excited nucleus only loses energy, A and Z stay the same:
⁵⁸₂₉Cu* → ⁵⁸₂₉Cu + γ
(Naming Z = 21 as scandium uses the periodic table; beyond the chapter.)

blocks.prompt: 12.5 Why neutrino must be released in the positron emission?
blocks.explanation: The emitted positrons have a continuous range of energies, though the energy released in each decay is fixed. A neutrino must carry away the missing energy (and momentum), so that energy and momentum are conserved (proposed by Pauli, 1930). It also balances the lepton number: the positron is an anti-lepton, the neutrino a lepton.

blocks.prompt: 12.6 Distinguish between fermions and bosons.
blocks.explanation: Fermions have half-integer spin and obey Pauli's exclusion principle; bosons have zero or whole-number spin and do not.

rows: Obey Pauli's exclusion principle: only one particle of a kind in a given quantum state
Do not obey Pauli's exclusion principle
Carriers of forces (field particles) and mesons
Examples: electron, proton, neutron, quarks, neutrinos
Examples: photon, pion, gluons, W and Z bosons, Higgs boson

blocks.prompt: 12.7 How does strong force hold the nucleus?
blocks.explanation: Protons in the nucleus repel each other electrically. The strong nuclear force attracts all nucleons alike (p-p, n-n, p-n) and, within its short range (< 10⁻¹⁵ m), is about 100 times stronger than the electric force. So it overcomes the repulsion and binds the nucleus. (It acts between quarks through gluons.)

blocks.prompt: 12.8 Can there be pair production for photons having energy 20 keV? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation: No. Pair production needs a photon energy of at least the rest mass energy of the pair, 2mₒc² = 1.02 MeV. 20 keV = 0.02 MeV is far less than 1.02 MeV, so an electron-positron pair cannot be produced.

blocks.prompt: 12.9 What is the difference between beta particle and electron?
blocks.explanation: A β-particle is an electron (or positron) created and emitted by the nucleus; an ordinary electron revolves outside the nucleus. Once emitted, a β⁻-particle is indistinguishable from an orbital electron.

rows: Created in the nucleus at the moment of decay (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄)
Already present outside the nucleus (orbital electron)
Emitted with very high speed, up to 0.9995 c
Bound in orbit with much smaller energy
Can be negative (β⁻, electron) or positive (β⁺, positron)
Is nuclear radiation (ionizing, range several metres in air)

blocks.prompt: 12.10 How do a proton and a neutron convert to each other?
blocks.explanation:
Neutron to proton (β⁻-decay): ¹₀n → ¹₁p + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄; in quark terms a down quark changes to an up quark (udd → uud).
Proton to neutron (β⁺-decay, inside a nucleus): ¹₁p → ¹₀n + ⁰₊₁e + ν; an up quark changes to a down quark (uud → udd).
Both changes are caused by the weak nuclear force.

blocks.prompt: 12.11 Why does beta-decay have a continuous energy spectrum and alpha-decay have a discrete energy spectrum?
blocks.explanation:
α-decay gives only two products (daughter nucleus and α-particle), so the fixed decay energy is always shared in the same way: every α-particle has the same sharp energy (discrete lines).
β-decay gives three products (daughter, β-particle and antineutrino or neutrino); the fixed energy is shared between the β-particle and the (anti)neutrino in varying proportions, so the β energy ranges from zero to a maximum (continuous).

blocks.prompt: 12.12 Differentiate between hadron and leptons with examples.
blocks.explanation: Hadrons feel the strong force and are made of quarks; leptons do not feel the strong force and are fundamental.

rows: Do not experience the strong force; interact only by weak and electromagnetic forces
Two groups: baryons (three quarks, fermions) and mesons (quark-antiquark, bosons)
Six leptons in three pairs; all have spin 1/2 (fermions)
Examples: proton, neutron, pion, kaon, lambda
Examples: electron, muon, tau and their neutrinos

blocks.prompt: 12.13 Why electron-positron pair cannot decay into a single photon?
blocks.explanation: Because momentum would not be conserved. For a pair at rest (total momentum zero), a single photon would carry momentum E/c ≠ 0. Two photons moving in opposite directions with equal momenta keep the total momentum zero, so e⁻ + e⁺ → γ + γ (0.51 MeV each).

blocks.prompt: 12.14 State the role of Higgs Boson in the generation of mass in modern physics theories.
blocks.explanation: The Higgs field permeates all space; particles get their mass by interacting with it. Particles that interact strongly (W⁺, W⁻, Z) get large masses, while photons do not interact and have zero rest mass. The Higgs boson (discovered at CERN in 2012, about 125 GeV) is the particle of this field and confirms the mechanism.

blocks.prompt: 12.15 What are Mesons? Give example.
blocks.explanation: Mesons are hadrons made of a quark and an antiquark; they are bosons (spin 0 or whole number). Their masses are mostly between the electron and nucleon masses. Examples: pions π⁺ (ud̄), π⁰, π⁻ and kaons (K).

blocks.prompt: 12.1 Why does Beta particle have continuous energy spectrum?
blocks.explanation: In β-decay a fixed amount of energy is released, but three particles share it: the daughter nucleus, the β-particle and the antineutrino (or neutrino). The share of the β-particle and the (anti)neutrino varies from decay to decay; their sum is always the same. So a β-particle may get any energy from zero (the neutrino takes almost all) to a maximum (the neutrino takes almost none). Plotting the number of β-particles against kinetic energy therefore gives a smooth curve, a continuous spectrum (Fig. 12.6), unlike the sharp lines of α-decay.

blocks.prompt: 12.2 Is meson or boson or fermion? Give reason.
blocks.explanation: A meson is a boson. It is made of a quark and an antiquark, each of spin 1/2; their spins combine to a whole number (0 or 1). Particles with zero or whole-number spin do not obey Pauli's exclusion principle and are bosons (they obey Bose-Einstein statistics). For example, the pion has spin 0. (Mesons are also hadrons, but not fermions; baryons are the fermion hadrons.)

blocks.prompt: 12.3 Why does an alpha emitter emit alpha particles instead of four separate necleons?
blocks.explanation:
An α-particle (2 protons + 2 neutrons, a helium nucleus) is an extremely tightly bound, stable group: forming it releases about 28 MeV of binding energy (beyond the chapter). When a heavy nucleus emits a ready-made α-particle, the products have less mass than the parent, so energy (positive Q-value) is released and the decay is possible.
To emit four separate nucleons, this binding energy would have to be supplied as well; the heavy nucleus does not have that much energy, so emission of four separate nucleons is energetically impossible. Also, inside a heavy nucleus nucleons tend to form α-clusters, which leave as one unit.

blocks.prompt: 12.4 Which is more energetic Alpha decay or Beta decay? Justify your answer.
blocks.explanation:
Alpha decay is generally more energetic.
1. α-particles are about 7300 times heavier than β-particles. Using the speeds in Table 12.2: K.E. of an α-particle = 1/2 mv² = 1/2 × 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg × (10⁷ m s⁻¹)² ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻¹³ J ≈ 2 MeV, while a β-particle at about 10⁸ m s⁻¹ (0.33 c) has only about 0.03 MeV.
2. Every α-particle carries the whole sharp decay energy (typically 4-9 MeV, beyond the chapter), while a β-particle carries only a part of the decay energy (continuous spectrum), the rest going to the (anti)neutrino.
3. This is why α-particles produce about 10⁴ ion pairs per mm in air against about 10² for β-particles. (β-particles are faster and more penetrating, but carry less energy.)

blocks.prompt:
12.5 A nucleus undergoes Gamma decay, emitting Gamma ray photon with energy 1.5 MeV. Calculate.
(i) frequency of Gamma ray
(ii) wave length of Gamma ray
(iii) momentum of Gamma ray
blocks.explanation:
Given: E = 1.5 MeV = 1.5 × 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 2.4 × 10⁻¹³ J
h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
(Photon relations E = hf and p = E/c are beyond the chapter.)
(i) Frequency:
E = hf, so f = E/h
f = 2.4 × 10⁻¹³ J/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s
f = 3.62 × 10²⁰ Hz
(ii) Wavelength:
λ = c/f
λ = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹/3.62 × 10²⁰ Hz
λ = 8.29 × 10⁻¹³ m
(iii) Momentum:
p = E/c (= h/λ)
p = 2.4 × 10⁻¹³ J/3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
p = 8.0 × 10⁻²² kg m s⁻¹
Answer: f = 3.62 × 10²⁰ Hz, λ = 8.29 × 10⁻¹³ m, p = 8.0 × 10⁻²² kg m s⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 12.6 Why does the a-particles not make physical contact with the nucleus when headed directly toward it?
blocks.explanation: Both the α-particle and the nucleus are positively charged, so they repel each other with an electric force that grows rapidly (as 1/r²) as the α-particle comes closer. Its kinetic energy is changed into electric potential energy; at the distance of closest approach its kinetic energy becomes zero and it is pushed back. This happens far outside the very short range (< 10⁻¹⁵ m) of the strong nuclear force, so the α-particle turns back without touching the nucleus (as in Rutherford's scattering experiment; beyond the chapter).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints 'a-particles'; it means α-particles (alpha particles).

blocks.prompt: 12.1 What is meant by radioactivity? Compare the properties and behavior of three types of radiations.
blocks.explanation:
Radioactivity: the spontaneous emission of radiation (α-particles, β-particles and γ-rays) by unstable nuclei. Nuclei with atomic number greater than 82 are naturally unstable (natural radioactivity); unstable isotopes made in the laboratory by bombarding stable nuclei with neutrons, protons, α-particles or γ-rays show artificial radioactivity (radioisotopes).
Behaviour in an electric field (Fig. 12.4): α-particles bend towards the negative plate (positive charge), β-particles bend more towards the positive plate (negative and lighter), γ-rays pass undeflected (no charge).
The comparison of their properties is in the table (Table 12.2).

rows: Electrons or positrons from the nucleus
Ionization (ion pairs per mm in air)

blocks.prompt: 12.2 Elaborate the phenomenon of beta-positive decay and beta-negative decay with examples.
blocks.explanation:
β-decay is the emission of a β-particle (electron or positron) from a nucleus. The β-particle is not an orbital electron; it is created in the nucleus at the moment of emission. No nucleon is lost, so A stays the same while Z changes by one. It is caused by the weak nuclear force.
β⁻ (beta-negative) decay: occurs in nuclides whose neutron-to-proton ratio is too large. A neutron changes into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino:
¹₀n → ¹₁p + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄   (quark level: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄)
General: ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ_(Z+1) Y + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄
Example: ²³⁴₉₀Th → ²³⁴₉₁Pa + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ (also ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄).
β⁺ (beta-positive) decay: occurs in nuclides whose neutron-to-proton ratio is too small. A proton changes into a neutron, a positron and a neutrino:
¹₁p → ¹₀n + ⁰₊₁e + ν
General: ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ_(Z−1) Y + ⁰₊₁e + ν
Example: ¹⁹₁₀Ne → ¹⁹₉F + ⁰₊₁e + ν.
In both, the energy released is shared between the β-particle and the (anti)neutrino, so β-particles show a continuous energy spectrum; the (anti)neutrino was proposed by Pauli (1930) to conserve energy. The two decays are compared in the table.

rows: Emits an electron and an antineutrino
Emits a positron and a neutrino
Z increases by one, A same
Z decreases by one, A same

blocks.prompt: 12.3 What is the difference between matter and antimatter? Discuss reasons why our universe is almost entirely composed of matter.
blocks.explanation:
Antimatter is made of anti-particles, which have the same rest mass as their particles but opposite charge (predicted by Dirac in 1928; the positron was found by Anderson in 1932). The differences are in the table.
Why the universe is almost entirely matter:
1. Observations show a matter-antimatter asymmetry: the universe contains hydrogen and helium atoms but no antihydrogen or antihelium.
2. Experiments indicate that this asymmetry is due to the violation of conservation of baryon number, i.e. an imbalance between the numbers of baryons and anti-baryons.
3. If particle-antiparticle symmetry is also violated, there is a mechanism for making more quarks than antiquarks and more leptons than antileptons, and so finally more matter than antimatter.
4. Wherever matter and antimatter met, they annihilated into radiation; the small excess of matter survived and forms the universe we see (beyond the chapter).
The exact cause of the asymmetry is still a mystery.

rows: Made of particles: electrons, protons, neutrons (quarks and leptons)
Made of anti-particles: positrons, anti-protons, anti-neutrons (antiquarks and antileptons)
Particles carry their usual charge (e.g. electron −e, proton +e)
Same mass but opposite charge (positron +e, anti-proton −e)
Written without a bar: p, ν
Usually written with a bar: p̄, ν̄
Makes up almost the whole observable universe
Very rare; made in cosmic rays and accelerators
On meeting antimatter it annihilates into energy (γ-rays)
On meeting matter it annihilates into energy (γ-rays)

blocks.prompt: 12.4 Explain the phenomenon of pair annihilation with an example. Explain the utility of its principle in the medical field.
blocks.explanation:
Pair annihilation is the opposite of pair production: when a particle meets its anti-particle, both disappear and their mass changes into energy (γ-ray photons) according to E = mc².
Example: e⁻ + e⁺ → γ + γ
For an electron and a positron nearly at rest, two γ-photons of 0.51 MeV each (total 1.02 MeV = 2mₒc²) fly off in opposite directions. Charge (−e + e = 0), energy and momentum are conserved; two photons are needed so that the total momentum stays zero. Other pairs also annihilate: proton and antiproton, quark and antiquark.
Medical use: PET (positron emission tomography) scan (beyond the chapter):
1. A positron-emitting radioactive tracer (e.g. glucose containing fluorine-18) is injected into the patient.
2. Each positron soon meets an electron in the body and annihilates into two 0.51 MeV γ-photons moving in opposite directions.
3. A ring of detectors around the patient records the pairs of photons at the same time; the computer finds the line on which each annihilation occurred and builds a 3D image.
4. Active tissues take up more tracer, so PET shows metabolism: it detects cancer and its spread, brain disorders and heart problems.

blocks.prompt: 12.5 Explain the law of conservation of energy and momentum in electron-positron pair annihilation.
blocks.explanation:
Reaction: e⁻ + e⁺ → γ + γ
Conservation of energy: the total energy before (rest mass energies plus kinetic energies) equals the total energy of the photons after:
mₒc² + mₒc² + K.E. = E₁ + E₂
For a pair nearly at rest: E₁ + E₂ = 2mₒc² = 1.02 MeV, so each photon has E = mₒc² = 0.51 MeV.
Conservation of momentum: for a pair nearly at rest the total momentum before is zero, so the total momentum of the photons must also be zero. A single photon always carries momentum (p = E/c), so one photon is impossible. Two photons of equal energy moving in opposite directions have equal and opposite momenta: p₁ + p₂ = 0. That is why at least two photons are produced.
Charge is also conserved: (−e) + (+e) = 0 = charge of the photons.

blocks.prompt: 12.6 Describe protons and neutrons in terms of their quark composition.
blocks.explanation:
Protons and neutrons are baryons (hadrons), each made of three quarks of the two lightest flavours: the up quark u (charge +2/3) and the down quark d (charge −1/3).
Proton = uud: q = 2/3 + 2/3 + (−1/3) = +1
Neutron = udd: q = 2/3 + (−1/3) + (−1/3) = 0
Each baryon has one quark of each colour (red, green, blue), so it is colourless. The quarks are held together by the strong (colour) force, carried by gluons (quantum chromodynamics). Quarks never appear on their own.
The quark model also explains β-decay: when a down quark changes into an up quark (d → u + e⁻ + ν̄), the neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud).

blocks.prompt: 12.7 Describe four fundamental forces in nature.
blocks.explanation:
All interactions in the universe are governed by four fundamental forces:
1. Gravitational force: the weakest (about 10⁻³⁸ of the strong force) but of infinite range; always attractive; proportional to the product of masses and inversely proportional to the square of distance. Significant for massive bodies (Sun, planets), negligible between atomic particles. Carrier: graviton.
2. Electromagnetic force: acts between charged particles; attractive or repulsive; follows the inverse square law; about 10⁻² of the strong force, infinite range. Governs atomic structure, chemical bonding, electricity, magnetism and light. Maxwell (1861) unified electricity and magnetism. Carrier: photon.
3. Weak nuclear force: about 10⁻¹³ of the strong force, range < 10⁻¹⁸ m. Responsible for radioactive β-decay and neutrino interactions; it can change the identity of particles (n ↔ p), essential for fusion in stars. Carriers: W⁺, W⁻ and Z bosons.
4. Strong nuclear force: the strongest (relative strength 1), short range (< 10⁻¹⁵ m), only inside the nucleus; attracts all nucleons alike and overcomes the repulsion between protons, holding the nucleus together. Carrier: gluons.

blocks.prompt: 12.8 Describe the classification of elementary particles.
blocks.explanation:
1. By spin:
Fermions: spin 1/2, obey Pauli's exclusion principle (electrons, protons, neutrons, quarks, leptons).
Bosons: zero or whole-number spin, do not obey it (photon spin 1, pions spin 0, gluons, W, Z, Higgs).
2. By the forces they feel:
Hadrons: feel the strong force; made of quarks. They are of two kinds:
   Baryons (heavy): three quarks; fermions; e.g. proton (uud), neutron (udd), lambda (Λ⁰), sigma, omega.
   Mesons (middle mass): a quark and an antiquark; bosons; e.g. pions (π⁺ = ud̄), kaons.
Leptons (light): do not feel the strong force; fundamental, spin 1/2; six leptons in three pairs: electron and electron neutrino, muon and muon neutrino, tau and tau neutrino, each with its anti-particle.
3. Fundamental particles (the standard model):
Quarks: six flavours, up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom, with fractional charges (+2/3 or −1/3).
Leptons: the six leptons above.
Bosons (force carriers): photon (electromagnetic), gluons (strong), W⁺, W⁻, Z (weak), the graviton for gravity (not yet observed), and the Higgs boson, which explains how particles get mass.
Each particle has an anti-particle. Matter (5% of the universe) is made of quarks and leptons.

blocks.prompt: 12.1 Uranium-238 is an alpha emitter. In the process, it is transmuted into a daughter nucleus. What is the mass number (A) and charge number (Z) of the daughter nucleus? What is its chemical symbol? (Ans: A-234, Z=90, Thorium)
blocks.explanation:
Given: parent ²³⁸₉₂U (Z = 92), alpha decay
Required: A and Z of the daughter, its symbol
In α-decay: A decreases by 4 and Z decreases by 2 (ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ⁻⁴_(Z−2) Y + ⁴₂He)
A = 238 − 4 = 234
Z = 92 − 2 = 90
²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He
Answer: A = 234, Z = 90; the daughter is thorium, ²³⁴₉₀Th (same as the book's answer).

blocks.prompt: 12.2 Polonium ²¹⁸₈₄Po is a beta minus emitter. What will be the mass number (A) and charge number (Z) of the daughter nucleus? (Ans: A = 218, Z = 85)
blocks.explanation:
Given: parent ²¹⁸₈₄Po, β⁻ decay
Required: A and Z of the daughter
In β⁻-decay: A stays the same and Z increases by 1 (ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ_(Z+1) Y + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄)
A = 218
Z = 84 + 1 = 85
²¹⁸₈₄Po → ²¹⁸₈₅At + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄
Answer: A = 218, Z = 85 (astatine, At; naming the element is beyond the chapter). Same as the book's answer.

blocks.prompt: 12.3 Nitrogen ¹⁴₇N bombarded by alpha particle results into ¹⁷₈O. What is the product particle in this nuclear reaction? (Ans: ¹₁H proton)
blocks.explanation:
Given: ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + ᴬ_Z X
Required: the product particle X
Nucleon number: 14 + 4 = 17 + A, so A = 18 − 17 = 1
Charge number: 7 + 2 = 8 + Z, so Z = 9 − 8 = 1
A particle with A = 1 and Z = 1 is a proton, ¹₁H.
¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + ¹₁H
Answer: the product particle is a proton, ¹₁H (same as the book's answer).

blocks.prompt: 12.4 Show that nucleon number (N) and charge number (Z) are conserved in the numerical question 12.3.
blocks.explanation:
Reaction: ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + ¹₁H
Nucleon number:
Before: 14 + 4 = 18
After: 17 + 1 = 18
18 = 18, so the nucleon number is conserved.
Charge number:
Before: 7 + 2 = 9
After: 8 + 1 = 9
9 = 9, so the charge number is conserved.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question calls the nucleon number N. By the book's own Eq. 12.1, N is the neutron number and the nucleon (mass) number is A; the conserved quantities are the nucleon number A and the charge number Z.

blocks.prompt: 12.5 Determine the rest mass energy of electron in eV. Its rest mass is 0.0000555 u? (Ans: 0.51 MeV)
blocks.explanation:
Given: rest mass of the electron mₒ = 0.00055 u (Section 12.1; the printed 0.0000555 u has an extra zero, see the correction below)
1 u = 931 MeV (Section 12.1)
Required: rest mass energy Eₒ in eV
Eₒ = mₒc² = 0.00055 u × 931 MeV/u
Eₒ = 0.512 MeV
Eₒ = 5.1 × 10⁵ eV ≈ 0.51 MeV
Check in SI units: mₒ = 0.00055 × 1.6606 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 9.13 × 10⁻³¹ kg
Eₒ = 9.13 × 10⁻³¹ kg × (3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)² = 8.22 × 10⁻¹⁴ J
Eₒ = 8.22 × 10⁻¹⁴ J/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ = 5.1 × 10⁵ eV
Answer: Eₒ = 5.1 × 10⁵ eV = 0.51 MeV (the book's answer).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints the electron's rest mass as 0.0000555 u. That value gives only 0.0000555 × 931 MeV = 0.0517 MeV (5.17 × 10⁴ eV), not the printed answer 0.51 MeV. The electron's rest mass is 0.00055 u (Section 12.1; more precisely 0.000549 u), which gives 0.51 MeV; the printed value has one zero too many.
